traces.input_message: Review the paper provided in your context and produce your structured assessment.
traces.system_prompt:
You are an expert peer reviewer for a top-tier machine learning conference.

Work in this order:
1. What the paper does: problem and claimed contributions.
2. Weaknesses first: identify the strongest objections on novelty, technical
   soundness, empirical evaluation, and clarity. Ground every objection in a
   specific section, claim or result of the paper as provided to you; never
   invent content. If you could not verify a claim because the relevant part
   of the paper was not available to you, say so instead of assuming it holds.
3. Strengths: what genuinely holds up, also grounded in the text.
4. Scores last: derive rating and sub-scores from the weaknesses and strengths
   above, not the other way around.

Rating (1-10): 10=award quality, 8=strong accept, 6=marginally above the
acceptance threshold, 5=marginally below, 3=clear reject, 1=fundamentally
flawed. Use the full scale: most submissions fall in 3-6; reserve 8-10 for
papers with no significant unaddressed flaw.

Sub-scores (1-4): 1=poor, 2=fair (notable gaps), 3=good (minor gaps),
4=excellent. Soundness: are the claims supported by correct arguments and
evidence. Presentation: is the paper clear, complete and well organized.
Contribution: how much it adds over prior work. A 4 is rare: give it only if
you could defend it in front of a skeptical colleague, and keep each
sub-score consistent with the weaknesses you listed.

Confidence (1-5): base it on how much of the paper you actually inspected and
on your expertise: 5 only with (near-)complete access to the text; lower it
when you judged mainly from a summary or a few retrieved passages.

Output: summary under 600 characters; significance_and_novelty under 300
characters; 1-4 reasons for acceptance; 1-4 reasons for rejection (at least
one unless the rating is 9 or higher: every real submission has a weakness
worth stating); 0-4 actionable suggestions. Suggestions are only for
improvements that did NOT affect your scores; anything that lowered a score
belongs in reasons for rejection. Each list item is one self-contained
sentence naming the section or claim it refers to.

- [calibration] Apply calibrated skepticism: hold the paper to the venue's real acceptance bar, where most submissions are rejected. Judge the substance of the evidence, not the fluency of the prose — polished text is not a merit in itself. Treat vague boilerplate, generic or unnatural phrasing, unsupported or unverifiable claims, inconsistent notation and other signs of low-effort or machine-generated writing as concrete weaknesses to name and weigh in your scores. When the evidence for a claimed contribution is missing, score as if the contribution were absent.
- [venue] The paper is a submission to the International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR). Apply ICLR standards: the conference values rigorous theory, strong empirical evaluation, and advances in representation learning, deep learning, and reinforcement learning; it runs an open review process, so reviews should be defensible point by point in a public discussion with the authors.

response_payload.summary: The paper presents a reinforcement learning framework for automated code refactoring that combines contrastive pre-trained graph embeddings with traditional code quality metrics. Experimental results show improvements over baselines in syntactic improvement, semantic preservation, and generalization, though computational costs and novelty compared to prior work are concerns.
response_payload.significance_and_novelty: Proposes a novel RL framework for code refactoring using contrastive pre-trained embeddings, improving over handcrafted rewards and expert demonstrations.
reasons_for_acceptance: The paper introduces a novel combination of contrastive pre-training and reinforcement learning for automated code refactoring, addressing limitations of handcrafted reward functions (Section 4).
The experimental results demonstrate significant improvements over baseline methods across multiple metrics, including syntactic improvement and semantic preservation (Table 1).
The ablation study effectively validates the importance of key components like contrastive pre-training and semantic preservation (Table 2).
reasons_for_rejection: The novelty of combining contrastive learning with RL is not sufficiently differentiated from prior work like GraphCodeBERT and SyncoBERT (Section 2.2).
The computational cost of contrastive pre-training is acknowledged but not thoroughly analyzed (Section 6.1).
The cross-language generalization results show only marginal improvements over rule-based tools (Table 3).
suggestions: Provide more detailed analysis of computational costs and scalability trade-offs in Section 6.1.
Clarify the novelty of the approach compared to GraphCodeBERT and SyncoBERT in Section 2.2.
Include more qualitative examples of non-obvious optimizations in Section 5.5.

response_payload.summary: The paper introduces a novel RL framework for automated code refactoring using contrastive pre-trained code graph embeddings. It addresses the challenge of balancing syntactic improvements with semantic preservation, outperforming existing methods across multiple datasets and metrics.
response_payload.significance_and_novelty: The paper's novelty lies in combining contrastive pre-training with RL for code refactoring, enabling automatic learning of code quality representations without handcrafted rewards. This approach significantly improves generalization and semantic preservation.
reasons_for_acceptance: The proposed method outperforms state-of-the-art baselines across all evaluation metrics, demonstrating its effectiveness (Section 5.2).
The contrastive pre-training enables faster convergence and higher final performance, as shown in the learning curves (Section 5.2).
The framework supports cross-language generalization, indicating its transferability to diverse codebases (Section 5).
The ablation study highlights the importance of contrastive pre-training and semantic tests, validating the design choices (Section 5.3).
reasons_for_rejection: The computational expense of contrastive pre-training, especially for large codebases, is a significant limitation (Section 6).
Scalability concerns are acknowledged, though the system supports up to 1 million lines of code, which may not suffice for industrial-scale applications (Section 6).
The paper lacks a detailed discussion of potential failure cases or scenarios where the method might underperform (Section 6).
suggestions: Include a broader range of programming languages in the evaluation to further demonstrate cross-language generalization (Section 5).
Provide a more detailed analysis of the computational trade-offs involved in contrastive pre-training (Section 6).
Discuss potential ethical considerations, such as the impact of automated refactoring on developer workflows (Section 6).
Explore the integration of additional semantic preservation techniques to further enhance robustness (Section 4).

traces.system_prompt:
You are the meta-reviewer of a top-tier machine learning conference. You receive the individual peer reviews of one submission and synthesize them into a single aggregated assessment for the Area Chair.

Structure your synthesis in this order:
1. Points of consensus among the reviewers.
2. Disagreements, and which side is better supported.
3. The decisive strengths and weaknesses after weighing the arguments.

Judge arguments, not just scores: a well-substantiated objection outweighs an unsupported enthusiastic rating. Do not introduce claims about the paper that no reviewer made and never invent content.

Overall score (1-10): the aggregated quality of the paper, consistent with the reviewers' calibrated scale (most submissions fall in 3-6).
Recommendation: accept (ready as is), minor_revision (real but fixable concerns), reject (fundamental flaws or insufficient contribution).

Output: summary under 600 characters; 1-5 key points, each a single self-contained sentence.

- [venue] The paper is a submission to the International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR). Apply ICLR standards: the conference values rigorous theory, strong empirical evaluation, and advances in representation learning, deep learning, and reinforcement learning; it runs an open review process, so reviews should be defensible point by point in a public discussion with the authors.

response_payload.summary: The paper proposes a reinforcement learning framework for automated code refactoring using contrastive pre-trained graph embeddings, demonstrating improvements in syntactic improvement, semantic preservation, and generalization over baselines. While reviewers agree on the novelty of combining contrastive pre-training with RL and the empirical improvements, concerns include insufficient differentiation from prior work, computational costs, and lack of comparison with recent deep learning baselines.
key_points: The paper introduces a novel RL framework for code refactoring that combines contrastive pre-trained embeddings, reducing reliance on handcrafted rewards and improving semantic preservation.
Experimental results show significant improvements over baselines in syntactic improvement, semantic preservation, and generalization, supported by ablation studies.
The novelty of the approach is questioned due to insufficient differentiation from prior work like GraphCodeBERT and SyncoBERT.
Computational costs of contrastive pre-training are acknowledged but not thoroughly analyzed, raising scalability concerns.
The evaluation lacks comparison with recent deep learning baselines, limiting the assessment of the method's relative performance.

You are an Area Chair of a top-tier machine learning conference. You receive the meta-reviewer's aggregated assessment (and, when available, the individual reviews and the author rebuttal) and must produce the final, binding decision on the submission.

Reach your decision in this order:
1. Check the meta-review: is its recommendation actually supported by the reviewers' arguments it summarizes?
2. Weigh the unresolved concerns: are they fundamental to the contribution, or fixable in a revision?
3. Decide independently: you are not bound by the recommendation — but justify any departure from it.

Base your decision only on the material you received and never invent content.

Decision: accept (ready as is), minor_revision (real but fixable concerns — the authors get a revision round), reject (fundamental flaws or insufficient contribution).
Confidence scale (1-5): 5=certain of the decision; 3=reasonably confident but the case is close; 1=highly uncertain.

Output: summary under 400 characters; justification under 400 characters, stating the decisive reason for the decision.

- [venue] The paper is a submission to the International Conference on Learning Representations (ICLR). Apply ICLR standards: the conference values rigorous theory, strong empirical evaluation, and advances in representation learning, deep learning, and reinforcement learning; it runs an open review process, so reviews should be defensible point by point in a public discussion with the authors.

traces.system_prompt:
You are the corresponding author of a paper under review at a top-tier machine learning conference. You receive the peer reviews (and the area chair's assessment when available) and must respond to them.

Respond in this order:
1. General rebuttal: your overall response to the review round.
2. One targeted response per reviewer, addressing their specific concerns point by point (use the reviewer's name as provided, e.g. 'reviewer_1').
3. Revise the sections the reviewers most convincingly criticized: for each one, produce the complete rewritten section text.

Concede valid points explicitly and say what you changed; push back on misunderstandings by pointing at the exact passage that answers them. Never invent results, experiments or citations that are not in the paper.

Only reference sections, numbers and results you have actually seen. If the paper text is not accessible to you, phrase revisions as commitments (what will be clarified, added or expanded) — do NOT invent section numbers, experiments, rewritten text or specific content.

Prioritize the concerns that drove the scores: fixing the decisive objection is worth more than answering every minor comment.

Output: general rebuttal under 600 characters; each per-reviewer response under 1000 characters; at most 3 revised sections; 1-5 key changes, each a single self-contained sentence.

response_payload.rebuttal: We thank the reviewers for their thoughtful feedback. We will clarify our differentiation from prior work, particularly SyncoBERT and GraphCodeBERT, by emphasizing our refactoring-specific contrastive objectives and RL integration. We will also expand on computational costs and efficiency trade-offs, and strengthen comparisons with baselines by adding ablation studies on reward components.

reviewer_rebuttals.response: We appreciate your positive assessment of our technical approach. To address your concerns: (1) We will clarify our differentiation from SyncoBERT and GraphCodeBERT by emphasizing our refactoring-specific contrastive objectives (structural augmentations) and RL integration in Section 2. (2) We will expand the computational cost analysis in Section 6, including pre-training time, memory usage, and scalability trade-offs. (3) We will add an ablation study on reward components in Section 5 to better understand their individual contributions.

Thank you for your detailed feedback. We will: (1) Strengthen the comparison with baselines by adding more detailed analysis of their limitations in Section 5. (2) Clarify the novelty of our approach compared to prior RL methods by emphasizing our self-supervised contrastive pre-training and embedding-guided exploration in Section 4. (3) Add a discussion of potential negative societal impacts in Section 6, focusing on misuse in code plagiarism and over-reliance on automated refactoring.

We thank you for your constructive comments. We will: (1) Add more implementation details, including hyperparameter settings and training time, in Section 5. (2) Clarify the semantic preservation mechanism by expanding the differential testing description in Section 4.5. (3) Strengthen the empirical evaluation by adding case studies that illustrate specific refactoring improvements in Section 5.5.

revised_sections.content: We will add a new subsection (2.4) explicitly comparing our approach with SyncoBERT and GraphCodeBERT, highlighting our refactoring-specific contrastive objectives (structural augmentations) and RL integration. This will clarify our differentiation from prior work.

We will add an ablation study on reward components to better understand their individual contributions. We will also include more detailed implementation details, such as hyperparameter settings and training time.

We will expand the computational cost analysis, including pre-training time, memory usage, and scalability trade-offs. We will also add a discussion of potential negative societal impacts, focusing on misuse in code plagiarism and over-reliance on automated refactoring.

Included ablation study on reward components in Section 5.
